steps.explanationAfterStep: The alkene attacks iodine and iodide leaves, as in bromination. The bridged iodonium ion forms on the face of the ring away from the CH₂CO₂⁻ group, because the carboxylate must then reach the opposite face. The step is reversible.

The carboxylate opens the iodonium ion from the opposite face: an anti addition across the C=C. A five-membered lactone closes onto the carbon next to the ring CH carrying the side chain, and iodine stays on the other carbon. The lactone is cis-fused to the cyclopentane (not checked by the app yet).
Also correct: the alkene attacks iodine as the carboxylate closes the ring, in one step. The anti addition and the five-membered ring are the same either way; the textbook shows the iodonium ion.

title: Iodolactonisation
subtitle: I₂ and an internal carboxylate add anti across a cyclopentene and close a γ-lactone
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 20 (electrophilic addition to alkenes; iodolactonisation)
E. J. Corey, N. M. Weinshenker, T. K. Schaaf and W. Huber, Stereo-controlled synthesis of dl-prostaglandins F2α and E2, J. Am. Chem. Soc., 1969, 91, 5675–5677

reactants.caption: the sodium carboxylate of the hydroxy acid + I₂ (as I₃⁻ in aqueous KI)
hintTiers: Like bromine, iodine is an electrophile towards an alkene: the C=C π electrons attack it and an iodide leaves. A bridged, three-membered ion forms.
The C=C π bond attacks one iodine atom; that iodine uses a lone pair to bond to the other alkene carbon; the I–I bond breaks to give iodide.
C=C π bond → new bond from one alkene carbon to an iodine; lone pair of that iodine → new bond to the other alkene carbon; I–I bond → lone pair on the other iodine.
reactants.learnerPrompt: Iodine reacts with the C=C. Draw the first step.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The OH takes no part. The alkene is the nucleophile towards iodine; the carboxylate is the nucleophile that comes next.
An acyl hypoiodite (RCO₂I) can form, but it delivers I⁺ to the alkene in the same way. Draw the alkene attacking iodine directly.
Iodine is the electrophile here: the I–I bond breaks to give iodide, not to make a bond to carbon.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right so far. The other alkene carbon is now short of electrons: the iodine's lone pair bridges to it (one more arrow), or the carboxylate attacks it at once.

iodolactone.caption: the iodolactone: a cis-fused γ-lactone with iodine next to the CH–OH

iodonium-ion.caption: the iodonium ion, on the face of the ring away from the carboxylate
hintTiers: An iodonium ion is opened from the face opposite the iodine. A nucleophile in the same molecule wins over iodide in solution, and five-membered rings close fastest.
A carboxylate oxygen attacks the iodonium carbon nearer to its CH₂, closing a five-membered lactone (a γ-lactone); the C–I bond to that carbon breaks.
Carboxylate oxygen lone pair → new bond to the iodonium carbon next to the ring CH carrying the CH₂; that C–I bond → lone pair on iodine.
iodonium-ion.learnerPrompt: The carboxylate opens the iodonium ion. Which carbon does it attack, and what size of ring closes?

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Attack at the far carbon would close a six-membered, bridged lactone. The five-membered ring closes faster, and the γ-lactone is what Corey isolated.
Iodide can open the iodonium ion, but that diiodide simply reverts. The carboxylate, held next to the ring, closes the lactone instead.
The OH is a much weaker nucleophile than the carboxylate, and would close a strained small ring. Use the carboxylate.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: the five-membered lactone closes. That carbon now has five bonds: break its bond to iodine.

mechanismSummary: Corey opened the bicyclic lactone with aqueous NaOH to the sodium salt of a hydroxy acid: a cyclopentene carrying CH₂CO₂⁻, OH and CH₂OMe, all on the right faces. Iodine (dissolved as I₃⁻ in aqueous KI) reacts with the C=C to give an iodonium ion on the face away from the carboxylate. The carboxylate opens it from the other face, an anti addition, closing a five-membered lactone. The result is the iodolactone: a cis-fused γ-lactone with iodine on the next carbon. Iodolactonisation does two jobs at once: it sets the oxygen of the future prostaglandin ring OH on the correct face, and it protects the carboxylic acid as a lactone. Stereochemistry is explained here; the app does not check it yet.
